title: The transistor
matchup: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley (1947–1948) vs Lilienfeld (1925–1928)
question: Do Lilienfeld's patents and the evidence about working devices support Schmidhuber's proposed transistor invention credit?

usual_credit.summary: Standard accounts credit John Bardeen and Walter Brattain with the working point-contact transistor demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947, while William Shockley developed the junction-transistor approach. The [Computer History Museum](https://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/invention-of-the-point-contact-transistor/) describes their achievement as a successful semiconductor amplifier, rather than the first proposal to control semiconductor current with an electric field. The [1956 Nobel citation](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1956/summary/) recognizes semiconductor research and discovery of the transistor effect, and the museum separately credits Atalla and Kahng with the successful insulated-gate field-effect device developed in 1959 and demonstrated in 1960.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that Julius Edgar Lilienfeld's earlier field-effect designs justify calling him the transistor's inventor, and that the Nobel award should have recognized him. He cites Robert Arns's historical account, later reconstructions of Lilienfeld devices, and Bell Labs' knowledge of the patents to argue that these were workable inventions rather than unimplemented suggestions. His broader argument also stresses the importance of field-effect transistors in later electronics, which is a different issue from priority for the point-contact transistor.

response.summary: The [Computer History Museum](https://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/field-effect-semiconductor-device-concepts-patented/) acknowledges Lilienfeld's field-effect patents but says contemporary records establishing working devices are absent. It distinguishes those concepts from Bell Labs' working point-contact amplifier and from Atalla and Kahng's later practical MOS transistor, which addressed semiconductor surface-state problems. Schmidhuber cites reconstructions and historical reports as evidence for the earlier designs' feasibility. Those reports and the museum's requirement for contemporary evidence address different standards of proof; the linked material does not include the original Bardeen letter or Arns's full article, or a direct reply to Schmidhuber's 2025 argument.

agreed_facts: Lilienfeld's US1745175A records priority on 22 October 1925, a US filing in 1926, and a grant in 1930: https://patents.google.com/patent/US1745175A/en
Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated a working point-contact semiconductor amplifier in December 1947: https://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/invention-of-the-point-contact-transistor/
Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain shared the 1956 Physics Nobel Prize: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1956/summary/
crux: The dispute concerns whether invention credit should follow an early field-effect design, evidence that the design could work, or the later demonstrated transistor effect and practical devices. Priority for a field-effect concept, priority for a point-contact transistor, and the merits of a Nobel citation are related but do not have identical criteria.

card.headline: The transistor
card.question: Should Lilienfeld's 1925 field-effect patents make him the inventor of the transistor?
card.claim: He says Lilienfeld's field-effect designs worked as described and gave substantial gain, so Lilienfeld invented the transistor and deserved the Nobel Prize.
card.pushback: The Computer History Museum says no records prove Lilienfeld built working devices, and credits Bell Labs with a working point-contact amplifier in 1947.
card.crux: The question is whether credit goes to an early patented design, to later evidence it could work, or to a demonstrated device.
